utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This morning Judge Williams is unable to proceed with us due to urgent personal reasons, but we shall continue the proceedings, because we consider it to be in the interests of justice to do so, under the provisions of Rule 15 bis. Ms. Reidy, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mrs. Kapetanovic, I just have a few more questions for you about things put to you by Defence counsel. You were asked about the incident with a former neighbour of yours, Vera Avdic, and the stove that you saw her unloading from her tractor, and you explained how that linked into your experience when you had to loot houses. Did you loot houses or loot property from Croat and Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely from Muslim and Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you were instructed to remove the property from those houses, did anybody tell you that they were being removed from the houses so that they could be returned to their rightful owners?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not told that, but just to leave the items along the road, in an orderly manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You were asked also a question about the time that the ICRC visited Zasavica, and you were asked about whether or not you addressed Mr. Simo Krunic, who was there. Did you also address the ICRC delegates in English directly yourself?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I addressed them in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So as well as speaking to Simo Krunic in B/C/S, you spoke -- or you communicated to the ICRC delegates directly in English?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You were also asked about an obligation to participate in harvesting, which you -- this was asked you by counsel for Blagoje Simic. For this work obligation to harvest, did you receive any form of payment whatsoever for carrying out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you performed the harvesting, were you exclusively with other persons of Muslim and Croat ethnicity or did you also conduct this harvesting with members of the Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among women, I was the only Catholic, and the others were Muslim. And amongst men, there were Muslims and Catholics. I've never seen Serbs working.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you conducted this harvesting, were you supervised by armed guards in military or police uniform?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military and police uniforms, the armed guards were always along with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And finally, just two or three questions on more issues raised by counsel for Blagoje Simic. Are you or have you, at any time, ever been or been asked to be an agent for the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, neither in the past nor during my freedom, when I gained my freedom, after the exchange, nor today. I don't know what it means to be an agent.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: After you were exchanged, Mrs. Kapetanovic, did you try to make money by weaving baskets?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only way to earn money, in order to pay my way to Zagreb, in order to go for my check-ups. It was the first time that I began doing this. My fingers were all bleeding, and I was helped at the time by my then boyfriend, whenever he was free.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So you didn't go into the pay of the Croatian government, then, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Otherwise I wouldn't allow myself to do such work.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The information which women were able to bring back to all of you persons isolated in Crkvina, was this kind of gossipy information about what they witnesses in their villages, in their houses, when they went back to collect food?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information related exclusively towards -- exclusively to the fact whether their houses had already been looted or had they been burned. So this information related to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the information that you conveyed to the people on the other side when you were exchanged, was this a normal procedure? You said talking to people who were responsible for civilian authorities about how you had been treated whilst you were in Bosanski Samac and what your personal experience was.

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely a normal procedure which applied to us who had been prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Finally, Mrs. Kapetanovic, I take it that Pegi was your only pet, was she? You didn't have any carrier pigeons or any other mode of communicating with the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two parrots, who died two days after I had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the parrots used for communicating any information to the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JELENA KAPETANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, these parrots didn't talk yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's the end of my cross-examination -- re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Kapetanovic, for giving evidence to the Tribunal. You are now released. You can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yesterday after the proceedings the Trial Chamber was informed by the Registry that -- by Mr. Christian Rohde from the Registry that Mr. Sredoje Novic should be given audience before the Trial Chamber because he has been accepted by the Registry, although he's a legal assistant, to replace Mr. Vukovic, the co-counsel. So Mr. Pantelic, Mr. Novic can have audience whenever it suits you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, for this information, and I think that Mr. Novic will take part in some of the cross-examination coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The other matter the Trial Chamber wanted to give its ruling on the documents that were discussed on Friday, D25/4, attachment number 1, copy number 2, and attachment number 2, copy number 2, and attachment number 3 of this document will not be admitted into evidence. The Defence can discuss them further if they so wish during the Defence case. Although they are attached to D25/4, the three attachments have separate topics and can be severed from the rest of the document which forms D25/4. D26/4, with its counterpart in terms of B/C/S, this document is also admitted into evidence. The weight to be attached will be considered with the totality of the evidence at the conclusion of the trial. D42/1 with its counterpart will still remained as identified. It will not be admitted into evidence. The next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is ready, but I need some guidance on the Trial Chamber as to whether or not the written statement of this witness, which was accompanied by a declaration pursuant to Rule 92 bis subsection B is to be admitted in part -- is to be admitted into evidence as part of this testimony, as that would obviously dictate how I would examine in chief this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Has it been filed?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say "filed," my understanding from last Thursday's discussion, or Friday's discussion, was that I would file it through the Senior Legal Officer, and I did. By filing it, meaning through Senior Legal officer so that the Judges would have their copies and it was so done. A written motion didn't accompany it because I understood Your Honours to say that that was not necessary and there would simply be a ruling on Tuesday. I did have a draft motion to file --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Later on the matter was discussed by the Trial Chamber with the Legal Officer, and instructions were given that the statement should be actually filed. Because the statement we have, which was given to us does not have the declaration attached to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I handed up the statement with the declaration attached, which is in B/C/S, and the English translation with it. The 92 bis version has, in the bottom right-hand corner, the stamp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. The B/C/S version has the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's correct. That's one that the witness has read and signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the English version is obviously provided for the purposes of the official language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. I just want to hear from the Defence. They had the statement served on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can confirm that we have the -- yes, on behalf of all Defence team, I can confirm that we were provided with the B/C/S version of the statement, witness statement, in accordance with the Rule 92 bis, as well as the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is identified. But, Your Honour, for the sake of clarity, I would like to draw the attention of this Trial Chamber, and also maybe we could have some clarification from the -- our learned friends from the Prosecution, since we are entering into the, I would say, a new area in this trial proceedings with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- Rule 92 bis, and I kindly ask you to forgive me if I will give certain comments which might be very useful. I mean, instructions from this Trial Chamber for the coming proceedings. In fact, Your Honour, I would like to draw the attention of this Trial Chamber, and also ask for some clarification from my friends, with certain method how we should proceed with this kind of documents. Point number 1, Your Honour: We are in possession, we, Defence, are in possession of two B/C/S versions of this statement, signed by witness Mr. Jasarevic Osman. These two versions are slightly different because one version, B/C/S version, has internal numbers on the upper right-hand side; the other version, although signed, hasn't this kind of ERN numbers. So that's first difference, and I would like to hear from the Prosecution which, in fact, version it will be introduced during the examination-in-chief, also in the cross-examination. Another matter which I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you leave that topic, the two versions, are they dated the same date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same date, and they both signed by same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can clarify this point first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. I am guessing at what Mr. Pantelic is referring to, but my guess is that what he's talking about is that the minute the statement was signed in B/C/S, it was copied and disclosed to Defence. We then entered it into our evidence vault, at which stage it gets assigned an ERN number. That is a numbering with which the Bench will be familiar. All it is is a stamp put in the right-hand corner so that internally we can retrieve that document, et cetera, from the system. I believe my case manager, out of a matter of protocol and thoroughness, also gave a copy later to the Defence also with a document with the ERN number in the corner so they know what the ERN number is. There is no difference whatsoever between the actual statements that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's one and the same document except that the other one has ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Exactly. And whichever version the Court would like to take into evidence is a matter for the Bench. We have both available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's much easier to deal with the one with ERN numbers, because then you can discuss the pages clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. It is very important, and it will be very, very important for us to make this reference. And my understanding as well is that these two versions are completely same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I said, so we take that these two signed B/C/S versions, one with ERN number, the other without ERN number are practically the same. So that's our conclusion and our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But for purposes of the trial, we shall use the copy with ERN numbers, because it's much easier to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Point number 2, Your Honour: Probably the Bench is in possession of B/C/S version and English version of Mr. Jasarevic Osman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you be so kind, Your Honour, to just take a short look on, for example, page 1 B/C/S version, which is the last three digits are 510. This is actually the -- in B/C/S version. On the upper right-hand corner, in B/C/S version -- well, it means in English probably "draft translation." I think that maybe it's an omission or it's a kind of typing error, or I don't know to which category I will assign this two words. But since we've been yesterday in quite a situation which was not so clear with regard to the version English and B/C/S version, now I would like to clarify that prior to beginning of the testimony of this witness, from the Prosecution, to see whether it is draft translation or it is official translation or which version we have in B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because I take this -- this particular B/C/S version is signed by the witness, but nevertheless, there is a note there that it's a draft translation in B/C/S. And then, for example, Your Honour, if I'm going to cross-examine this witness, I will make reference, of course, to his native tongue, and then my learned friend will say, "Well, we don't have that in English version," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So in order to avoid and to spare our precious time, Your Honour, I would like to clarify that now with my learned friend from Prosecution. And thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So these words which mean draft translation are on the statement with the ERN numbers, the one we're going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The one we intend to use. All right. Explanation from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The reason that there is a draft translation in the corner is because this was originally a draft translation before the witness had an opportunity to have a look at it. It's been translated by an authorised translator from the witness unit. It did not come back from the revision process before the witness was here to sign the 92 bis procedure. However, the witness has read the statement, read through it carefully, and signed it. We are happy to go with this version. I do not believe that there are any differences between the English version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Is it the position of the Prosecution that these words meaning draft translation should actually -- should have been removed?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think they should have been removed after the witness had read the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that the position of the Prosecution is that the statement with the ERN numbers in Serbo-Croat is the official translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It's the official statement of the witness and what's in there he signed and read, and let's see if he stands by what's in there. I would also just for the record, since my learned friend brought it up, advise the Bench that I've shown to my learned colleague the revived version of yesterday's statement that was in dispute. It does contain the missing words about his client. So the revision process, in the Translation Unit, clearly picked up that oversight in the draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And that was accepted by Mr. Pantelic yesterday, that the English version actually was all right, and I can see him agreeing that it was a mistake to omit the sentence. So we shall treat this statement as filed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just wait, and we ask the Prosecution that they should get it filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you wish me to file it now by way of oral motion? That's what I understood that the Senior Legal Officer said that we could do to file it. Or would you wish me after our session this morning to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We take it that the discussions do indicate that the oral motion is on and then we grant it and just have it filed today. Because we're going to start using it. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Maybe I'm not interpret your words correctly. I agreed that it was a mistake to omit the sentence in B/C/S version, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are referring to yesterday's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To yesterday's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But I don't know who is in fact responsible for the discrepancies between B/C/S version and the English version. So I can confirm that after the analysis I found these discrepancies, and my idea was to clarify that with the witness. But if you think that, with your words, that I made a mistake, I respectfully disagree, Your Honour, that it was a mistake from my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, but Ms. Reidy has explained that the Translation Unit has agreed that they omitted the statement from the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my understanding. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I've just said that the statement will be treated as filed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, then may I hand you the ERN copy that so we'll all working off the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It is important that we are all looking at the same copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since we still have the time to deal with the general topics relating to statement under Rule 92 bis, I would like to go back to what I said on Friday, and regarding the next two witnesses, Mrs. Ediba Bobic and her husband Kemal Bobic, we only have draft versions of their statements, which have not been signed yet, and we said that once this statement has been given to the witness to authenticate and there are no significant differences, then that's fine. But if we only receive that on the day when we're supposed to cross-examine, then I think that our rights will be significantly affected, and we think that our clients need to be given draft versions in B/C/S in a timely manner. So we have not received any of the witnesses -- any of the statements under Rule 92 bis for any of the upcoming witnesses. My colleague Pantelic now just suggested to me, as a technical aid that would assist us in dealing with this in a more efficient manner, is to have the Prosecution mark to us any changes, any modifications that have been made, so that we can go through these statements in a quicker way. But we still insist that these statements need to be delivered to us at least several days before the witnesses are due to be examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, what is the explanation from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all, on the drafts that -- for the other witnesses' statements that have been given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to express some surprise and a bit of frustration about this. It's very clear that the reason that the Defence counsel do not have signed statements of the witnesses is that the witnesses have not yet arrived in The Hague and they have not been therefore available to go through the Rule 92 bis procedure. This was always going to be the case with the witnesses. I've had numerous discussions with Defence counsel about this, showing them calendars, which of course, because of the length of witnesses, have changed, explaining to them that witnesses would arrive, would sign their statements, would be disclosed to them, and hopefully they would have 48 hours in which to, you know, reread the signed statement. It was agreed that draft statements would be disclosed as soon as possible so that they had ample time to look through them, see any differences from the original statements that were given in 1995, et cetera. So the reason that the statements of the Bobics or of Witness A have not -- the signed versions have not been given to Defence counsel is because the witnesses have not yet arrived in The Hague to do so, and maybe at this juncture I should advise the Chamber that the first witness to arrive in The Hague will be Witness A, because the two Bobics have experienced the visa problem that I alerted the Court to, because their passports were issued before the 21st of June, 2001, I believe, and that puts them in a different category. So the Witness A will arrive on Friday. He will go through the 92 bis procedure. That will be disclosed to the Defence on the same day. They will have at least the weekend then to -- and obviously to file it on that day and they will have the weekend to compare that to their already disclosed, unsigned draft statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But can the Trial Chamber be assured that the drafts which are given to the Defence as soon as they are available will not differ from the signed statements? Because this is where the problem is, because it will undermine the rights of the accused in relying on that draft statement and giving instructions to the Defence counsel based on those draft statements. If the changes occur, then that will mean they haven't had sufficient time due to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I can't undertake such a guarantee that they won't change, because that's up to the witness when they come and reread it. But I can tell you that the effort -- every effort is made when these statements are taken, however difficult the circumstances, and with the interpreter, to make sure that it is an accurate reflection of what the witness has said. I do not believe that there has been any significant change in that of -- in the statement of Mr. Osman Jasarevic, who is due to testify. There was one change concerning the presence or not indeed of a -- or a conversation that took place with one of the defendants. In fact, it wasn't one of the defendants. It was a defendant's associate. But the changes tend to be minor and modalities of expression. Should there be a material change, that would of course be notified to the Defence and to the Bench, and we would not -- we would then -- the Bench said they would rule on a case by case basis as to whether or not it was more appropriate therefore to continue viva voce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I have also got instructions from the Senior Legal Officer that with the motions we should try to indicate if there have been any changes between the draft and the signed statement and that will certainly be undertaken and we can make references to paragraphs where there are changes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- that the witness desires. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the procedure will be once the witness comes and the particulars are taken and then the application will be made for the statement to be admitted or whatever the Prosecution wish to do with their statement. So can we have the witness brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the registrar to produce to the witness the signed statement recently filed, bearing the ERN number 01369509 through to 01369541.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sir, is your -- could you state your name and date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Osman Jasarevic. I was born on the 17th of November, 1950, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jasarevic, you'll see in front of you a document. Could I ask you to have a look at that document briefly and to see whether or not you identify it as your statement and a statement that you recently signed here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the document that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask that the document be given an exhibit or identification number at this stage so that it's clear for the record, any references made to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any objection. It can be admitted as the full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P129 and P129 ter, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you were born and brought up in Bosanski Samac from a family who had been established quite a long time in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My family, my father, my mother, my ancestors were all born in Bosanski Samac. My family was among the first to inhabit that area that is now known as Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you lived there with your family, including two sons, in 1992; that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I had two sons. The older one, Ahmet, was born on the 27th of August, 1977, and the younger one, Moamer, was born on the 29th of May, 1980, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, for the record, your eldest son, Ahmet, was he born on the 20th or the 27th of August? Because I think your statement you said it was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the 20th. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: That's no problem. I just wanted to get that clear for the record. Thank you. I'm going to ask you about some people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, I was just wondering, because all this information you're asking the witness is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour, and I apologise. This is the first time that I have a witness under this procedure, and my understanding was that we would have a limited examination-in-chief just to establish a little bit about the witness and the oral evidence about acts which would go to the acts and conduct of the defendants, including, of course, any mental elements of the crimes of which they're charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's only in a part, I think, where oral evidence can be given.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And of course any documents we wish to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, having established that, Your Honour, I'm just going to proceed to ask the witness if he's familiar with the defendants.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I need to ask you about some people, to see if you know them. I need to ask you about Mr. Blagoje Simic. Did you know Mr. Blagoje Simic, who used to live in Bosanski Samac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I know him, Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether you see him in this court today, and if so, could you describe for the record where he's sitting.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He's sitting in the middle, between Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think the record can reflect that Mr. Blagoje Simic has been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I take it, then, from your answer, that you're also familiar with both the personalities of -- or both the persons of Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And did you know them in 1992, in April 1992, when you were living in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you've said that Mr. Blagoje Simic was sitting between the to men. Could, for the record, you tell us which of them is sitting on which side of Mr. Blagoje Simic. Just make it clear for us who is who.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic is sitting to the right of Blagoje -- or rather, to the left of Blagoje, looking from here.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So from -- to your right, but on Blagoje Simic's left; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And then Simo Zaric is the third gentleman to the right of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think the record can reflect that the defendants have been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I first want to ask you some details about Mr. Miroslav Tadic. Are you familiar with -- that he was -- of a cafe that he was the owner in Bosanski Samac in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that cafe, and I know that he was an owner of the Cafe AS, Miroslav Tadic, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: In the time period of 1991 and 1992, did you have much occasion to go past or indeed visit Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I never entered the cafe, but I passed by the Cafe AS daily, because that was on my way to work. I would go to work in the morning and go back home in the afternoon and pass by the Cafe AS.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you used to pass by the cafe, did you notice anything about the clientele who used to go there, whether or not they were members of the military or any particular group?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: There was a gambling place there too, so a lot of gamblers would normally frequent that place, and all members of the 4th Detachment, as well as members of some special forces that were in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. These special forces you mentioned in your answer, what do you mean by "special forces" exactly? Could you explain to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were special forces that came when Samac was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were they from locally or were these -- when you say that they came when Samac was attacked, were these forces from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: They came from Serbia. They were not locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you witnessed these people in and around Cafe AS prior to the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in front of Cafe AS, in front of the cafe. I would normally see almost all members of the 4th Detachment, Simo Zaric, Fadil Topcagic, Djuric Avdo, Tota Ramusovic Nizam, Tota, these are the people that I would normally see there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned this 4th Detachment a number of times. Do you know whether the defendant Simo Zaric had any particular connection with the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He founded the 4th Detachment, and he was the main person in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And on what basis would you say that he founded the 4th Detachment? What was your reason for reaching that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was the only one who had some links to the State Security Service. He had retired from the State Security Service and he had contact with the Brcko garrison, with Stevan Nikolic, Kriger, who was in charge of that area. So he was a go-between between the army and the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Simo Zaric making public statements on behalf of the 4th Detachment or conduct any public activity on behalf of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: There were several public gatherings, rallies in Samac, in the cinema, in a square downtown, at which Simo Zaric held speeches, as well as others who volunteered to give speeches. Simo Zaric explained that the 4th Detachment was there to defend Samac. He said that his 4th Detachment was there to defend Samac from the army and from the enemy. However, the 4th Detachment was the one that opened the door for those Serbian paramilitaries and the army to enter Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. We know from your statement that you performed your JNA military service. Did Simo Zaric ever approach you to join this detachment simply for the defence of the town?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, nobody approached me about joining the 4th Detachment. After completing my military service, during which I served in the navy for two years, I was a member of the reserve police force. Simo Zaric, at the time, frequently held lectures for the reserve police forces about enemy from outside and the traitors, and later on this came to pass in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness identify the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can he identify the time when these things were happening, as he has alleged in his answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The last open gathering before the fall of Samac was seven days before Samac fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, this is this open gathering now, you're talking about the public gatherings which Mr. Simo Zaric spoke at and talked about the 4th Detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I'm talking about these gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And during which period of time did you receive lectures from Simo Zaric about threats and external enemies and traitors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That was before, before any conflict, in peacetime, when these lectures were mandatory for the reserve police force, to which I belonged. I was a member of the reserve police force. And I think that a month or two before the events I was removed from the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just explain to us the grounds on which you were removed, or were you given any reasons as to why you were removed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: They said that it was due to my age.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, do you recall an incident you've mentioned in your statement where two boys of Muslim ethnicity were killed in Cafe Valentino?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the vicinity of that spot because my wife worked in a shop in that part of the town. I was waiting for her. I heard a detonation, and all of a sudden a panic ensued. Young men fled from the cafe. They broke the window of the supermarket. And it was a state of general panic. I didn't know what was going on. Later on I learnt that at the time two young men had been killed, Bobic and Hadzialijagic, Mensur. Both of them were Muslims from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After that --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You can proceed. That's what I was going to ask you. Were you present then at a spontaneous gathering in front of the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: If you could perhaps -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I wanted to tell you, the owner of the cafe, Prole, told me that it wasn't the first time that the patrons were playing with the hand grenade and that they had deliberately activated the hand grenade and it wasn't a case of somebody throwing a bomb into the cafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, and my learned friend from Prosecution, I do apologise for interrupting the proceedings. It is not objection to this particular issue which my learned friend is pursuing. It's rather the understanding of the Defence when we started with the 92 bis procedure, our understanding was to expedite proceedings, to cut certain time, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Agreed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that light, we, as Defence, we think that we have all details in this particular witness statement here. Given the fact the other experience, in the other proceedings, where, in order to familiarise this witness with the proceedings, you know, obviously they have certain -- it's normal, new environment, et cetera, not more than 10 or 15 minutes to short explain what is in the statement and then we are going to cross-examine the witness. Otherwise, Your Honour, I really -- and my colleagues agree with me, we really don't see any sense with 92 bis statement. And then why -- what we have? A kind of combination viva voce and 92 bis standards? Or maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- you can give us more detailed instructions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because you know, Your Honour, to speak about the atmosphere, with all due respect, family background of this witness, and the other witnesses, atmosphere in Samac, accident in Cafe Valentino, not to -- not to mention the terrible events against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. I think your point has been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Rule 92 bis clearly states that - and the Appeals Chamber has made this clear as well - that evidence under Rule 92 bis can be given in part written and in part oral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It also clearly states that where there are aspects of evidence which go to the acts and conduct of the accused, including aspects -- material aspects of the Prosecution case and aspects of the mental state of any of the defendants, including, obviously, knowledge of things, that that also is not something purely for written format under 92 bis. Having the statement in front of us will expedite the matter. It will help with a lot of the background information which normally witnesses provide to the Bench. But with respect, I feel that the Prosecution must be allowed to lead viva voce evidence on incidents where the defendants are directly involved. In this incident, as it's clear from the statement, this incident was followed by a confrontation between -- I wouldn't say confrontation. That's a misclarification, but meet at a situation -- encounter. Thank you. An encounter between this witness and one of the defendants and indeed the witness has evidence that this encounter was later brought up when he was detained and interrogated. Now, to ask one question about whether he remembers the incident which gave rise to this encounter is not abusing Rule 92 bis. We are, as I said -- witnesses have taken up to three days here, three, four days longer before this Chamber. We hope 92 bis, it can be done maybe in a day. I don't know how long the Defence intend to cross. But I don't think that anything I've done so far, albeit it's a completely new way of proceeding with the witness, breaches the spirit of Rule 92 bis rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the problem is outlining what amounts to activities of the accused in this case, and that is left to the Prosecution. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, the statement -- it's part of the evidence of the witness, the activities of the accused and other matters accepted under Rule 92 bis have to be given orally, but as much as possible briefly, because the witness is here for cross-examination. And if the incident being discussed somehow has already been stated in the statement, it should be discussed orally as briefly as possible. Actually, indicating how it connects with the activities of the accused as charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That is what I will endeavour to do, and had Mr. Pantelic not interrupted, he would have seen it's clearly, clearly linked to the incident, the encounter where the witness meets Mr. Zaric. It's all contained within one paragraph, paragraph 25 of the statement, which Mr. Pantelic has had for many weeks now, and it's clear the linkage was there. So I think perhaps the intervention of Mr. Pantelic was somewhat premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I think he was right to intervene, because he wanted clarification which areas should be viva voce, which may be contained in the statement, but whose details have to be given viva voce because of the exceptions of Rule 92 bis. So his intervention was quite proper.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Well then for the benefit of Mr. Pantelic, it's paragraph 25 of the statement, and the link with the defendant is there. So perhaps that should indicate to him why it would fall under the exception of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that will help us, if you indicate the paragraph to which the viva voce evidence is alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a suggestion. We are all now first progressing in this manner. I think it would be very useful if the Honours set a limit also for us when cross-examination, and setting us a time limit, so that we could all focus on individual issues. This, I believe, would be good for us and also for the Prosecution. So this is how I understood also the initial instructions of the Bench, and I think that would be useful indeed for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree partially with the intervention of Mr. Lukic as to timing each party as to how much time they will take, but I do understand that the Prosecution may need, according to the way they understand their case, enough time to go through the activities of the accused and the matters excepted in Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And also, from the Prosecution's position is that, you know, we would oppose any strict limitation of time. We are going to endeavour to get through this as fast as possible and stick to the spirit of Rule 92 bis. However, many of the times the witnesses have taken a long time it's because of Defence counsel cross-examining for much longer than they said they would, et cetera. We don't know, with objection, et cetera, how long it might take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed and see how we fare.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, if you can remember where you left off after this procedural discussion. You had talked about being in the vicinity where two young men had been killed, Mr. Bobic and Mr. Hadzialijagic. Can I just ask you: After you had realised this incident occurred, did you proceed to the front of the SUP building, where people had gathered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went towards the SUP building because I already saw that a bigger group was gathering there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you were in front of the SUP building, did you meet one of the defendants there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were people shouting, mainly members of the 4th Detachment, and Fadil Topcagic, Ramusovic, Nizam Tota, Dzuheric Avdo, Simo Zaric, Mihajlo Topolovac, Radovan Antic, all of them were members of the 4th Detachment and all of them were shouting that a blue Lada vehicle, it was from there that this hand grenade was thrown, and a blue Lada would imply the Brcko licence plate, and therefore there was the policeman. The policeman even broke some doors. At a certain point, Simo Zaric said a commander of the city should be appointed. And as I knew what really happened, I told Simo -- I told him, "You would all like to be commanders of the city." And that was what was thrown back at me when I was interrogated by Milos Savic after I was being arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. You said here that a blue Lada would imply the Brcko licence plate. That's at least what's recorded in the statement. Do you mean that the blue Lada had a Brcko licence plate and that would imply something about the driver of the Lada?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What would a Brcko licence plate --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: A driver -- because a Brcko licence plate belonged mainly to Croatian villages towards Orasje, so it would have to be a Croat, and that is why it was presented, as if the Croats launched this hand grenade, place the blame squarely on them and to create havoc. And I recognised this, these special forms of war, intimidation, unrest, and that was something also that Simo Zaric lectured about when I was still in the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. Just for the record, from the question that my learned colleague Ms. Reidy asked. The question was: "Do you mean that the blue Lada had a Brcko licence plate?" It could suggest that this witness actually saw a certain blue Lada with Brcko registration plates, and he never actually said that, so maybe she clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Reidy, you heard Mr. Lazarevic's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you clarify for us, Mr. Jasarevic: Did you see a blue Lada with a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Reidy, but isn't that quite clear from paragraph 26, who said and who indicated what? It was Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. That's my reading of it. But I've been asked to clarify by Defence counsel and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, perhaps you could just turn your statement to paragraph 26. If you could find paragraph 26. Do you see paragraph 26?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you see a sentence in there that says: [As read] "He circulated the story that a blue Lada with a Brcko licence plate, indicating that it was therefore a Croat had thrown a bomb into the cafe"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And is that what you meant? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely that is what I wanted to say. That's why I put it down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Just to concentrate again on that paragraph, just to clear the record: You said that you spoke with Simo Zaric and said that no one threw a bomb. Did you also tell him that no one had thrown the bomb, as well as telling him --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I clearly stated that nobody threw the bomb and that I spoke with the owner of the cafe. And immediately after that, there was a formal statement that nobody launched the grenade but that those persons activated the hand grenade themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, I'd like now to take you up to the events of the 16th and 17th of April, and perhaps you could just turn to your statement, paragraphs 31 and 32. In those paragraphs, you describe taking your family out of Bosanski Samac on the evening of the 16th of April and yourself returning to Bosanski Samac on that same night. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And you were at home by yourself in Bosanski Samac on the evening from the 16th to the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the morning of the -- I ask you to look at paragraph 34 of your statement, and I understand that on the morning of the 17th of April, 1992, you had left your house early.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... witness to certain movements of people in Bosanski Samac that morning that you've described in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, did you learn that Bosanski Samac had been taken over by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: On that night when the police station was taken over in Bosanski Samac, I was at my apartment, at home. I heard the shooting and a few detonations, and these were Zoljas, hand grenades; I didn't know at the time. And in the morning I went to work. Usually I go to work very early, 5.30 a.m. or even earlier. Then I passed along the health centre. An ambulance was stopped there. A person was taken out. That was Ilija Vuckovic, a Croat, who was killed; and his son, who was a reservist in the police force, was wounded. And then I was looking, and somebody from the darkness said, "Do you also want to be killed?" Then I turned around and went home, and I stayed in my house up until 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasarevic. Can I just stop you there? It is in your statement that you then, about 9.00 a.m. in the morning, went out again to find your family, and that is at paragraph 36. Could I just ask you to look at your statement and see if that's correct? Paragraph 36.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I couldn't contact by phone my brother and my mother, there where they lived, around 9.00 a.m. I tried to reach them by foot, because they lived close by the police station. That was two streets further down. I went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, all that is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: -- along the road --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I know. I was going to indicate to the witness that it's in his statement, so I'll jump to it and bring him to another paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please. Do it such that the witness is not led to believe that he has it repeat what is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you said the -- what you began to describe, is that -- paragraph 36 of your statement, is that correct? I'd just ask you to look at paragraph 36. And then throughout your statement, to paragraph 40, you discussed --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- your movements through the town of Bosanski Samac that morning.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to move on to paragraph 41 of your statement, and you say that on Saturday, the 18th of April, members of the 4th Detachment, working together with Serbian special forces, were looking for weapons. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were -- the 4th Detachment and the special forces of Serbia were looking for weapons. However, at that day, at that time, I wasn't at home. I was with my neighbours, in view of the fact that I was alone. And then Dragan Delic, who was living above me, said that they came to the building and were searching for weapons. He was afraid that some problems would arise. Therefore, I called the police and handed over my weapons. I had a hunting rifle and a carbine. I had also the permits. They took over the rifles and threw away the papers, there right on the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. After you had handed over those two rifles, did you have any other weapons or anything else in your house that could cause you to be --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any other weapons except for those two hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see counsel on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a clarification. In the statement, it says that he handed over one rifle, and that's also in the statement -- and Ms. Reidy asked whether he handed over two rifles. And here in the statement we have one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a carbine rifle and a shotgun rifle, and these are two rifle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So -- yes. You said that you had no other weapons remaining in your house after you had handed over the carbine and the hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Notwithstanding you had handed in your rifles, did you receive information from your brother that the 4th Detachment had still come to his place looking for you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were looking for me, and they were looking for weapons from my brother, who was also a hunter. And they also took all his weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, I understand that on the 20th of April, 1992, you were arrested. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The details of your arrest are before the Court in paragraph 47 of your statement, and perhaps I could ask you to turn to that paragraph just so we all find the same statement. Were you arrested by both members of the special forces and a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was having lunch at my aunt's place, and I then had a nap. They came, they called out my name. I reacted. I saw a person -- a red beret. He wore also the insignia of the Serbian eagle and a cockade, and a member of the 4th Detachment, Niksa Bjelic was with him, and they asked me to come in for interrogation. I boarded their car. Later on I heard that this Vuk -- man was Vuk, who hit me, Vukovic, who hit me in the face with -- I was bleeding -- with my fist -- with his fist, and I was bleeding, and that is the way in the shape I was in when they brought me into the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At the time you were arrested, apart from being told that you were to come for interrogation, were you given any explanation as to why they were interrogating you, or did they explain to you any information about why -- any suspicions that they had about your activity?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I received no explanation, just a fist in my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And that fist came from this Mr. Vukovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later on I heard that his name was Aleksandar Vukovic who hit me with his fist in my face. Later, when he was killed, Vuk's foundation was set up in memory of this person. It was a foundation set up by the Crisis Staff, Foundation Vuk. And later on, a village was named Vukovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived upstairs, in your statement you explained that you were taken upstairs to the SUP building, to a room which looked onto the garages behind the SUP. Is that correct? And it's at paragraph 53 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to that I was taken to see Stevan Todorovic. Some special forces were there, with painted faces. They were beating me a bit. Stiv kicked me with his leg. And then they took me to the other part of the building, where the garages are. There they placed me at a table. I thought that they would be interrogating us. On that table I could see my hunter's knife, in which I also engraved my name. It is how I understood that they had entered my apartment, because that knife was in my hunter's jacket. The moment I sat down, Vuk hit me with a police baton on my head, and instinctively I raised my hand. There were ten of them. They all came -- closed in on me. One of them placed a pistol in my mouth. The other ones -- another one fired a pistol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. After all these months of our work here, the Defence - I'm speaking on behalf of all my colleagues - were never cross-examined any of the Prosecution witnesses with regard to the details, beatings, and all other events in police station, and that is a fact here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We think that these people here are absolutely not responsible for any of these, you know, crimes in SUP or with these special forces, et cetera, et cetera. That's the line of our Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we have now here 92 bis statement. This witness is going into the details about special forces, what did -- who did what, and when, et cetera, et cetera. We think that it's absolutely useless for these proceedings. We have all details here in the statement. We have repetitive statements of previous witnesses, and now we have to move on to substantial matters, Your Honour. Otherwise, I really don't see the reason why we are using 92 bis and not viva voce. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Thank you very much. Now that the Defence has stated what their case is, Ms. Reidy, it's much easier. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm very glad that that's the Defence case. Of course, the Prosecution case is the opposite, that these people worked together with the special forces. We've been trying to put evidence to that effect, and it's our case that that's what happened. It's clear in the indictment. Mr. Pantelic has still not conceded that we've established the allegations and the charges, for example, 16 subparagraph B about the beatings. He's completely just said -- his client has no responsibility. So while again we'll try to shorten it, we do need to put on the record, or in evidence, incidents of people having been beaten, as we allege in the indictment, and by people who we allege were working together with the defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. This document here is the admitted as the exhibit. We have a number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My learned friend can, in closing arguments, in whatever stage of proceedings, make relation exhibit -- with regard to the exhibit that this paragraph is related for possible link, et cetera, et cetera, kind of theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these people are not right people to be here. We have a special forces, we have a local criminals. They should sit here, Your Honour, not these people with regard to these beatings and all these tragic events. That's the position of Defence, and all artificial relations that Prosecution try to make is false. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pantelic. We shall take our break and I hope that during the break the Prosecution will revise their way of looking at the case against the defendants. We'll continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I? I will not revise my case with respect to the defendants, but if I could approach the witness during the break, I could perhaps speak with him about how I'm conducting the examination and try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You can do that when we resume at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We object. We firmly object to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has already informed the Prosecution, Mr. Pantelic. Let's have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, in view of the submissions of the Defence, and also having considered the fact that the witness is available for cross-examination, the Trial Chamber has decided that for all the matters that are already in the statement, you don't need to go over them, even if they include the activities of the accused. Because the reason for the exception here is it was contemplated that it was a situation where the witness was not being presented for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: From the very start of this procedure, it was contemplated that we would accommodate the Trial Chamber in taking the statements in severing Ms. Reidy from the trial team and sending her down to Bosnia on those weeks on end to get those statements, in the hope that it would speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We have been repeatedly assured by the Trial Chamber, repeatedly assured by the Trial Chamber, that we would be permitted to lead evidence where the evidence covers the direct activities of the defendants, and furthermore, and I remember this so very distinctly, so very clearly, saying to Your Honour - I believe maybe Ms. Reidy may even have left on her mission on that occasion - that we couldn't physically take down all the documents, and furthermore, that we would not be able to proof the witnesses and include in their statements material relating to the documents. And so having been assured by the Trial Chamber that we would be permitted to lead evidence directly from the witnesses of -- where it touches directly upon the activities and actions of the defendants, and secondly, the documentation, the Prosecution did its utmost to accommodate the wishes of the Trial Chamber, notwithstanding that it was not obliged to. That has our understanding for the last I can't recall, month and a half --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Since the matter was discussed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Since the matter was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And of course it's a matter of serious and, let me say, gravest concern to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- that these witnesses come into this Court, the first thing they encounter, if that procedure is to be adopted, is Defence counsel, the horrors that they have endured for months on end don't get an airing except for on a piece of paper. And it's -- on the other hand, the Prosecution is mindful, extremely mindful, of the need to get the case moving, and so on, and because of that we have, as I have already said, accommodated the Trial Chamber as much as we possibly could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's therefore with very -- with alarm that I hear that Your Honour says that we cannot lead evidence directly and simply bring in a witness and have to answer questions from Mr. Pantelic and so on. That will, A, have the effect of effectively gutting any ability of the Prosecution to lead important points, emphasise important points. The Trial Chamber will only ever see these witnesses when they're being cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic, and so on, and the ability of the Trial Chamber to form any meaningful assessment of the credibility of these witnesses will be seriously, seriously undermined. And so I urge the Chamber to reconsider any suggestion that we do not lead any evidence at all in examination-in-chief. The way things are going at the moment, it's, in my submission, extremely likely that we will finish the Prosecution case by the end of the month, by the end of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I haven't finished, Mr. Pantelic, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to say that we'll finish the Prosecution case by the end of July, then we'll come to summer break, and so on. And it's taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's not the point. I think the point we have to discuss is the manner in which these witnesses will be led --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And, of course, on that point we have no quarrel and we will try to accommodate the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because what was envisaged by the Trial Chamber is the part of the evidence which does not touch the activities of the accused will be in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In which case, the Prosecution would lead oral evidence on the activities of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it happens that the witness is available for cross-examination, and this particular statement does also include activities of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In part. Of course, I think it doesn't discuss whatever documents you wanted to discuss with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, of course not. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That can be done. That will be allowed. The only problem seems to be that having the statement with the activities of the accused already in it, it seems to be a waste of time to go over them unless there are particular issues that the Prosecution wishes to highlight by discussing them orally with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But the problem with that is that was not the understanding of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The understanding of the Prosecution when we embarked upon this 92 bis procedure was that we would be given freedom to lead all the evidence where it directly touches upon the activities of the accused and that the rest of the evidence, the background material and so on, would not be led. Now, that effectively will speed up matters. Now, I didn't realise that -- and I don't think my colleagues realised that when we took these statements, that we -- that the activities of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- direct activities of the accused, we couldn't lead evidence on that, or that there would be some further limitation on that segment of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. What I'm saying is this statement in particular, the one that we have for the witness, it does include the activities of the accused, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. This appears to be the problem because originally it was envisaged that these statements would not include that. Now that they include that, there's no need to go over them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. No, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the witness will be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, then we have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then, when we come to exhibits, whatever exhibits you want to discuss with the witness, that is okay. You can go ahead and deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, all I can say is that then the Prosecution has been operating under a misapprehension, because we thought that we would be permitted to lead evidence, in toto, in full, completely, where it directly involved activities of these defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But where that evidence is already contained in the statement, because perhaps there was a problem in severing that evidence from the rest of the evidence because of the way the witnesses speak, there is no need to go -- to reiterate it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, may I just have a moment to confer with my colleagues, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Would Your Honours just bear with me one further moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry to add to this. Your Honour, the reason that we are adding all the statements and all the information and activities of the defendants is not just because of 92 bis but also because of the rules of discovery. If we are to delete from those statements the statements, the activities, the actions of the defendants on 92 bis statements, then we will be in a violation of the discovery rules, the due process rules, and the rules of fairness, which technically fall through all of the rules of procedure, before this case or any other case. What we will do is we will have to, in our 92 bis statements, remove any statement or action of a defendant. These Defence counsel will immediately get up and object, claiming discovery violations, claiming that they're being ambushed, that we're not filing full statements, which will then force us to do something a little bit different, file a 92 bis statement and then, in addition to that, a discovery statement, where we'll list statements of each of the defendants, statements of actions, which then it becomes almost ridiculous. What we would like to do is file one complete statement and then highlight, if you want to call it, the actions of the defendant. Because the Rule of 92 bis clearly indicates that it does not apply to -- it goes to matters other than acts and conduct of the accused as charged in the indictment, and that's right in the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what you're forcing us to do, if we want to highlight during direct examination strictly those acts, those statements, those comments of each defendant, we have an option here. We can delete those from the 92 bis statement and then have a discovery violation or delete them from the 92 bis statement and file a 92 bis statement and a discovery statement, which is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no, Mr. Weiner. We don't have to go through all that. It's just that where the statement contains even activities of the accused, as this statement appears to contain, the Prosecution can go through those activities briefly. Because it appears to the Trial Chamber that the details are here in the statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it appears. However, here's the situation, Your Honour: Number one, that still seems to violate the Rule, be in direct violation of the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But that is a situation where the witness is not called for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
