utterances.text: I agree with that, but that's still -- that's how the Rule was originally established, when a witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But in addition, in addition, the other part of that is some of these statements, as to the actions of the defendant, in relation to the statements that a defendant made, are going to be contested, and you, as fact-finders, are going to have to determine where the credibility lies, who you should believe, who you should not believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the fact that these people didn't have a chance to get up there and explain their statement in relation to the actions of the defendant, explain them in detail, on direct, it is -- it hurts the Prosecution, because you don't get a chance to see them fully, to make a full decision, a complete decision, as to their credibility. All you're going to hear is some cross-examination, and which would probably force us to do an extensive re-direct, which would have been our direct examination. So we should be able to at least get into any actions and statements of the accused, because it has to be fair for the Prosecution as well as the Defence, and it has to be a full statement to go in, so it's fair to you, as fact-finder, so you can make that determination as to credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I'm grateful to Mr. Weiner for having raised that issue, but if you look at Rule 92 bis, it seems that the matter is settled, in the Prosecution's submission. It says: "A Trial Chamber may admit, in whole or in part, the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony, which goes to proof of a matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused." So it's absolute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's absolute. The provision is absolute, in my submission. There is no compromise that can be reached. As soon as we go -- as soon as we touch upon the acts and conduct of the accused, as charged in the indictment, then it's got to be oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So I think that that must mean that we can only lead oral evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the activities of the accused as charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. And it is certainly the position of the Prosecution that even if the Rule didn't exist, that's what they would want to do. But it seems to me that the debate must now be put to rest, because the Rule is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a few words, if I may add. Our understanding is that if we shall adopt the standard just proposed by our learned friends from the Prosecution, then the notion and the spirit of Rule 92 bis will never existed. Then we shall not have Rule 92 bis; we shall have some hybrid of examination-in-chief, viva voce testimony, then cross, re-direct, stuff like that. I mean, my suggestion -- I respectfully suggest to this Trial Chamber to have all forthcoming witness statements in -- based on Rule 92 bis, and then for each particular testimony, the Trial Chamber will have a view and then will give instructions with regard to the issues which should be covered and the length of examination, and stuff like that. I mean, this is a living matter, Your Honour. We are all aware about that. We cannot put all these particular statements in one box and say that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that would be my suggestion for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another thing. Your Honour, frankly, after reading all these statements based on the 92 bis Rule - there are several of them, five, six, I don't know - believe me, Your Honour, and I really stand on it. All these statements are repetitive and nothing new is in there with regard to the defendants, and we think, Your Honour, that with this active approach, we should finish this case in seven working days, seven working days will be enough to finish the case and then it will be the end. Because there is nothing new substantial in this new witness statement with regard to certain events, certain position of events. They are all the same, more or less the same. So that is the position of the Defence. Of course we are mindful of the concern of our learned friends. We don't want to undermine principle of fairness and cooperation and good spirit which we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But here I think the Trial Chamber will have the final word and final voice with regard to all this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, if I might just reply to Mr. Pantelic, it's difficult to imagine a more misconceived interpretation of Rule 92 bis than what he has just proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It is not for the Trial Chamber to pick and choose which bits it wishes to hear; it's for the Prosecution to present its evidence, just as it is for the Defence to produce the evidence to the Chamber that it wishes to produce, so long as, of course, it is relevant and so on. Secondly, I just can't understand, if Mr. Pantelic has read or has not read Rule 92 bis. I don't want to repeat it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, what you are trying to say is you are repeating your earlier submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I had hoped that it had been heard, but apparently it had not, so I just thought I had to re-emphasise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. It is just that. Mr. Pantelic had to be given the opportunity to make his own submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And as for the assessment of seven days, that is, I think judging from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We would look forward to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Indeed, we would, but given the history of the last eight months and the length of cross-examinations, I rather doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief, Your Honours. I firmly agree with what my colleague Pantelic said and I just wish to reply to what I heard Mr. Di Fazio say at the beginning. It is something that concerns me. It is very clear to us that both the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence specifically set forth that it is important to pay attention to the rights of victims in the proceedings. However, we may not take that as a criteria and have somebody who comes here to testify, even if that person is a victim, be allowed to have his rights fully upheld in this matter. I don't think that there should be a direct examination if a 92 bis had been taken from that witness. So we don't think that that person should be directly examined and then cross-examined. The standard that we are about to establish today should apply to the Defence witnesses as well, and the Defence is prepared to allow its witnesses, who will come here to testify under Rule 92 bis to be cross-examined immediately and not to be examined in chief first. The statement of a witness and a victim exists in the written form, and this is why I oppose the direct examination of such witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view and has decided that the Prosecution will be allowed to lead evidence which touches on the activities of the accused, even though the statement may contain the same in detail. They will be allowed to do so brief, as briefly as possible. They will also be allowed to discuss whatever exhibits they wish to discuss with the witness because that was not done at the time that the statement was being taken and thereafter the witness will be presented for cross-examination. The Prosecution can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could I ask the registrar if the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit P25 ter. That would be the B/C/S version. For the purposes of the Bench, and for the record, this exhibit is a decision of the Crisis Staff dated the 27th of June, 1992, on the establishment of the Aleksandar Vukovic Vuk Foundation. It bears the seal of the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo, and is signed by the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But you have referred this morning to your knowledge about the establishment of a Vuk Foundation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. This was announced on Radio Samac, the fact that this foundation was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Number one, this witness doesn't have any personal knowledge of this document, of this exhibit; number two, it is a well-established fact that he was released, he was exchanged, prior to the date of this decision. So I don't see any particular reason that this witness will go into the examination of this particular document. I do object on this basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The Prosecution will go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you heard about the fact orally. This Mr. Aleksandar Vukovic, was he one of the persons who beat you in the room in the SUP building upstairs when you were made to sit at the table, the incident you've described in your statement at paragraph 53?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Aleksandar Vukovic beat me the most. He was the first one who started beating me, and he broke a stick or a baton over my head, after which he started laughing. He said my head was so hard that it broke his baton.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I just ask you to have a look at this document. Have a look at who took the decision, who signed the decision, and advise the Chamber whether this corresponds to your personal knowledge of the establishment of this foundation and the man in whose name it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, objection, on the same basis. Now with regard to the profound way of examination. This witness clearly said that he never saw this decision, so I don't know -- I don't see a reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you've already been overruled. You allow the Prosecution to go ahead. After the evidence is given, if you still feel the same, you can refer to it in your closing arguments. Ms. Reidy, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, does this decision that you see in front of you correspond with the knowledge you have about the establishment of the foundation for the man who beat you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. This was announced on Radio Samac, the fact that the foundation had been established and who were the founders.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm now finished with that document before this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'd like now to move to the incident described at page 59 and 60 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've just realised the witness does not have in front of him his own statement. Could I ask that it be provided to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. The one that he himself has signed, Your Honour. For the record, it's P129 ter. It's paragraph 59 and 60, Honours, of the ... That's page 11 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, at one stage of your imprisonment were you taken from a small cage-like cell and dragged into the corridor on the upper floor of the SUP building in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did take me up there, where Izet Izetbegovic, Hadzialijagic Safet, and Pavo already were.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The Bench has before it, Mr. Jasarevic, your description in paragraph 59 of how you were beaten in the corridor that evening. Can you look at your statement and just make sure you're following it? This was the beating that you received from people you call Laki, Kico, Japan, and others. Have you found that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like to concentrate on is your knowledge of where Mr. Simo Zaric was when this beating was occurring. Did this beating occur in front of an office in which Mr. Simo Zaric was sitting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat me in front of the office where Simo Zaric sat. The door was upholstered. It was opened by force and not completely closed. I heard the conversation, but I couldn't see the other person he was talking to because the door was only slightly open.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So I understand you heard Mr. Simo Zaric in conversation with an unknown other party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: As well as hearing the conversation, did you yourself catch sight of Mr. Simo Zaric through the door, or was it only his voice that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I heard his voice and I saw him as he spoke on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you about the conversation you first overheard. What was the topic of this discussion that you overheard?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The first topic was that -- to the person that he spoke to, and I couldn't see, he told this person that a woman who worked at the kiosk across his cafe was a Croat and spied on them and conveyed all of the information that she thus acquired to her husband, who was a Croat from Prud, which was in Croatia. He also spoke on the telephone about exchange with Luka Gregurevic, and another Croat, who was supposed to be exchanged for two Serbs. Later on, Luka was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you being beaten in and around the same time that this conversation -- these conversations were ongoing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They beat me there for some two hours. They took it out on me and screamed. They stood on my hands, which were quite swollen, and hit me with baton on my head and back. The other two also kicked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you let out sounds while you were being beaten, screams or moans?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I did not. I did not let out any sounds. I didn't scream or moan. I simply concentrated on something else, which helped me, and this is how I came to overhear that conversation. This helped me diminish the pain and everything else that I was experiencing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the men who were beating you saying things to you, making insults to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: They didn't question me about anything. They simply told me I would be swimming in blood. They kicked me, hit me with batons, stood on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did the beating that you underwent create a lot of noise and commotion, so people would have heard the beating?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It did. Every time they gave me a good beating, they would start yelling out loud, "Get up, get up," and I would get up and then they would knock me down again. They were yelling, talking loudly. So anybody could hear it, not just people in that room, but everywhere around it, because they screamed so much and yelled for me to get up. So they would beat me, yell at me to get up, and then once I got up, they would kick me anywhere they could, in my chest, stomach, face, and then knock me down again onto the corridor floor. And this could be heard everywhere. Two men, Savo Cancarevic, police commander, stood a few metres away and watched a bit as they beat me, as well as Milos Culapovic, called Culap. He stood also some 2 metres away while they beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And these two persons you mentioned, you saw them standing there, did you, with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was facing them. I was down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have one clarification to seek on your statement. You mentioned a Luka Gregurevic, who was later killed. Was he later killed in the massacre in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was he a police officer who had been on duty the night of the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Luka Gregurevic was duty officer at the station, and he turned the station over to the Serb forces that night, or morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, the Trial Chamber has before it again the details of how you were placed back in the room and how you were later transferred across to the Territorial Defence building, and the beatings that you witnessed and experienced whilst you were in the Territorial Defence building. So I'd like to ask you just about some incidents, and it's -- when I say "incidents," it's the day on which you were taken back to the SUP building for interrogation. When you were brought across for interrogation, what injuries did you -- had you sustained already from your treatment up to that date in detention?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I had bloody swellings under my eyes, in my ears; my hair was all bloody; everything around my neck was bloody, on my chest; my hands were black and blue; my nails, my palms were black and blue from the beating by batons. I was all black and blue and bloody.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I understand you appeared before a gentleman called Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milos Savic ever inquiry with you about why you looked the way you did, how you had sustained any of those injuries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask me anything about my injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did he ask you anything about whether or not you had illegal weapons in your possession?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask me about any weapons, either legal or illegal. He asked me about a cannon that I made for the religious community, who issued a permit for me to make that cannon. And I think that he took out the questions from a list that had been drawn up by Simo Zaric. He asked me about saying to Simo Zaric that all of you want to be commanders now. He also asked me what my opinion about the Yugoslav army was. He didn't ask me anything else specifically about my other activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What gave you the impression that the questions were from a list into which Mr. Simo Zaric had had some input?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Because I only said this to Simo, and Milos Savic could not have known what I said to Simo. And he took out some papers, and something was written down there. He asked me about the cannon, who had issued the permit for me to build the cannon, and then he asked me about what my opinion was about the Yugoslav army, and I didn't tell him anything about that. He also gave me some statements to sign, which I did, but I was barely able to hold a pen in my hands. I couldn't pull my fingers together as I was signing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was what you signed ever explained to you or read out to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Nothing was read to me or explained. He simply said it was all over and that I would be sentenced soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did he tell you what you would be sentenced for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't tell me anything about why I would be sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in the SUP building being interrogated, could you hear screams of other people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I did hear. At one point Milos Savic left the office and told the guard to remain by the door. He left. Later, I heard screaming, noise, calls for help from the neighbouring room. Later on, I learned that Salko Hurtic had been beaten there so severely that that office, that room, was completely bloody. Other people had to go and wash that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, in your statement you have described the murder of one of your co-detainees, a man called Dikan. I'm not going to ask you to repeat that incident because the Judges do have your explanation of how poor Dikan was killed on the 26th of April. However, is it correct that you were moved out of the Territorial Defence building to the Brcko barracks soon after Dikan was murdered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was moved that night to the Brcko barracks, belonging to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: At the time of your transfer, did you see Simo Zaric present?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him. Simo Zaric came, as did Mihajlo Topolovac. Simo Zaric wore a uniform of a senior officer. I think that's what it was. Mihajlo Topolovac was with him. They made a list, called out our names, put us into a military truck. Everybody's names were called out except for Izet Izetbegovic; Luka Gregurevic; Baja, from Domaljevac; Orsolic; and Mate Pejic, I think. They remained in the TO. Luka and Pejic were killed later on in Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. When you got onto these -- this truck, did some of the detainees visibly need assistance to climb onto the truck because of their injuries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Most of the detainees had a very difficult time getting on the truck. The truck was quite high off the ground. I had great difficulty getting on the truck, because my ribs had been broken and I was unable to move my right arm. We also had to get Grga up, to lift him up to get on the truck, because he was unable to do that on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you recall whether, when Mr. Simo Zaric was there calling out the names, that the state of these detainees, including yourself and the man you called Grga, would have been very -- would have been evident? Was he there when people were getting onto the truck and would have witnessed how these persons looked like?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Anybody could see the condition we were in. While we were beaten at the TO, we were not allowed to clean the blood off ourselves. The blood was everywhere: On our faces, everywhere on our bodies. People were unable to move. And those who were less severely beaten had to help me get up on the truck as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, again, your statement is in evidence with the Judges, so they know about your transfer to Brcko and the conditions in which you were held, but I'd like to ask you to go to your statement, to paragraph 95, and I'd like to ask you about the incident you described there, where again, whilst in detention in Brcko, you had a meeting with the defendant Simo Zaric. Have you got -- you've got the paragraph. Mr. Jasarevic, how did you learn that Mr. Simo Zaric was present at the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that somebody, a captain probably, came to fetch me. His arm was in plaster. And previously I had seen him in Samac. His arm was in plaster as well. So he came to fetch me and took me to the office of Stevan Nikolic, where Simo Zaric, Fadil, Lazo Trojan, and some other people that I didn't know, already were sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was it explained to you the reason that you were brought to the room to meet these men?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Simo told me that he had promised my aunt he would bring me back to Samac, alive. Fadil told me right away that they would put a uniform on me and that I would spend some time with him, until my injuries healed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you spent some time with him, do you mean in the company of Fadil Topcagic, outside of detention, or how did he mean that you would spend some time with him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What sort of uniform did they say that they would put on you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He said he would take me to his house in Samac, put a uniform on me, and keep me there until my injuries healed. Well, they would put their uniform on me. That actually meant that I had to go over to their side, to join the 4th Detachment that was still in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did Simo Zaric ever suggest to you that you could simply be released from detention and live as a free citizen back in Bosanski Samac, as you had before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. He said I would go back and live as a free citizen, but a free citizen in their uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So do I understand that it was a condition of your release that you would join the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I think that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you accept the offer to join the 4th Detachment and in that way obtain freedom?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to accept that offer at any price and go back to Bosanski Samac, because the others were in a very difficult situation, and I was afraid they would kill them, so that I would become their informant or I'd be the one blamed for that. They have used these methods before. This is how they used Pasaga. They used him while he was useful to them, and later on, he had to spend several years in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: When you say the others were in a difficult position, do you mean the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I mean the other detainees who were with me in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And when you say that you were afraid that the others -- that they would be killed and that you would become their informant, were you afraid the impression would be given that if you left with Mr. Topcagic and Zaric that you had provided them with some sort of information about activities that the other detainees were alleged to have committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must admit that I did not understand this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, I don't know, but I was reading in front of me, and I still don't understand what our colleague wants this witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you've said that you were afraid that the other detainees would be killed and that you'd be the one blamed for it. And my question was directed at finding out why you thought that might happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to object to that. He never actually said that he would be blamed for killing of the other detainees. He said that he was afraid that he was going to be used as informer.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Or "I'd be the one blamed for that." It's at line 6 of page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think what -- yes. Ms. Reidy, just clear that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, were you scared that you would be blamed for other detainees being killed on the basis of information that it would be alleged you had provided?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I was afraid of, although there was no information to provide. They already knew everything about us. However, they used these kinds of methods to provoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst you were before Simo Zaric and the other men in the room, what sort of injuries did you have and what were the conditions of the clothes that you were wearing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten even more severely that night. Lugar beat me up. I barely survived. I had a bloody -- totally bloody -- the arcade [As interpreted] was also broken, and my kidneys were injured. I showed Simo the blue and all the blue stripes on my back and bruises. I showed that to Simo.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: How did you show that to Simo?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: When we were going out from that room, when they were taking me back with other prisoners, I showed Simo -- I raised my shirt and showed the bruises on my back and in the area of kidneys. He saw that, but he didn't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you said that you had been beaten by Lugar. Can I just clarify? This was in the TO, just before you had been transferred, not in Brcko barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This was not in the TO of Bosanski Samac, not in the barracks of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the transcript again, Mr. Jasarevic. Can I confirm that the beating by Lugar took place in the TO of Bosanski Samac and not in the barracks at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the TO of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: You said you showed Simo your bruises. What was the state of your clothing when Simo Zaric saw you in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: As I described earlier, the clothing was bloodied. Everything, my hair was bloodied, around my shoulders, and on my face, traces of beatings, beatings which occurred the night before.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jasarevic, I'd like now to move on later to incidents that happened to you in 1992 in Bosanski Samac. After this, I know that you were transferred from Brcko, and then you spent some time in Bijeljina, and that you finally were returned back to Bosanski Samac. That's in your statement, and that statement is before the Judges. So I'd like to turn -- ask you to turn just to page -- paragraph 110, and could I just ask you to confirm: Is that your recollection that you believe that you were returned to Bosanski Samac on the 13th of May, and you spent another 12 days there before you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: During those 12 days, you witnessed and experienced a number of other beatings in detention; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I witnessed the beatings, and I was beaten also.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And the beatings were conducted, amongst others, by members of the local Serb forces; is that correct, including a man who went by the nickname of Obad or Hornet?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Obad, Hornet and other local ones brought, Sasa Maslic, who was from Bosanski Samac, and he brought in a list of persons that should undergo beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the man who brought in -- what you said was a list of persons who should be subjected to beatings, because the record -- it's not reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Sasa Maslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you can turn to paragraph 116 of your statement. You'll see that the beating that you and others endured is described and before the Bench. And this happened the exact day before you were exchanged; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The following day I was taken for exchange. However, I spent a day in the secondary school, and the following day, then I was taken for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your exchange took place across a river, where you were transferred, I believe, across the river from Zasavica to Dubica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Present at your exchange were two of the defendants, Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you just some details about the circumstances of your exchange. Were you the only Muslim amongst the persons who were to be exchanged that day?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the only Muslim that was exchanged from our municipality on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The other persons exchanged with you, were they all male Croats?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: All males and Croats from the surrounding villages and from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Had you seen these men previously detained in the secondary school during that day that you said you spent there prior to your exchange?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen these persons when I was brought in from the primary school to the secondary school, in the gym. All these people, all these Croats, most of them I knew. They were detained. This was called isolation, but it was, as I understood it, real ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The term "isolation," was that used by the people guarding these men?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They used this term, "isolation." They were guards, policemen, and members of the 4th Detachment, who had different types of uniforms from those which the policemen wore.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now just some details about the role of the defendants in your exchange. The defendants, they were actually present at the crossing of the river in Zasavica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. They were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who called out your names from the list of people who were to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic had the list in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would only like a clarification in the question, page 66, line 24, that the defendants were actually present at the crossing of the river in Zasavica. Did they also cross the river? I wonder, could we clarify that? Or if you want to, Your Honours, we can do it during our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it can be clarified now. Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I can certainly ask if the defendants crossed over with the detainees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I was going to come to that question, but anyway, could you just clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Were the defendants at Zasavica when you were crossing or did they actually cross the river with the detainees to the other side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The injured -- the defendants didn't cross. They stood by the truck, where we were, and they called out the names. And then they formed groups of five or six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And for the sake of clarity, maybe we should have more details. The notion "defendants" are very, very general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The names.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Which of the defendants are we talking about here, Mr. Jasarevic? I think you've mentioned them already.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Another point of clarification, on side 67 line 9. It reads: "At the crossing of the river in Zasavica." As far as I can see, and according to the map, there is no river in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: There's some confusion there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, maybe it would be easier -- you were put on -- were you transported from the secondary school to the village of Zasavica on the morning of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the River Bosna is quite close to Zasavica. We weren't taken to Zasavica; we passed by Zasavica. We moved -- and the river is half a kilometre or a kilometre away from Zasavica, and that was the place that the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask if the witness could be shown perhaps Exhibit P9, I believe it is. It's the map of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: There's a version where -- not a close-up version but a slightly broader perspective of the area.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I ask exactly which letter of the Exhibit P, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think perhaps the best one is P9A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Is that the same as the map D32/1?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'd have to check what D32/1 is, Your Honour, but I could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you show the exhibit to His Honour on the Bench so he can see it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's actually slightly different.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. The P32 one is [sic] a different map entered by the -- yes, exactly. No, it's a different map that was entered into evidence by Defence counsel. But I hope that if we put P9 on the ELMO, you'll be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, could you have a look at the map in front of you? Perhaps you could turn to your right and just look at the actual document itself on the ELMO, which is beside you. Mr. Jasarevic, if you turn right. You can take a minute to look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: As well, if the usher could supply Mr. Jasarevic with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The pointer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, perhaps you could find for us, if you can, the village of Zasavica. Is that where you were taken the morning of your exchange, through Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And as best as you can orient yourself, if it's on the map, can you show us just where the crossing occurred? Mr. Jasarevic, maybe I should ask you one question before that. The river running behind that - I think it's marked on the map the river Bosna - is that the river that you crossed over and that runs behind Zasavica village?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: River Bosna, close to Zasavica. You can't see it properly here on the map. Bosna, and the road, a road, and a gravel pit along the river. So this is a road which passes by Zasavica. This is the place where gravel is mined. And on the other side is the village of Dubica.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So it's -- could you just perhaps one more time take the pointer and mark, as best you can, where you think the crossing point took place. I know it may be difficult to orientate yourself on the map.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: This -- we went along this road where the gravel pit is, the place where the gravel was excavated. And on the other side is Dubica, and the place is called Neteka. This is Dubica and this was Neteka, and it was here that we crossed the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that maybe clarifies things. It makes it easier to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I was just because -- asking for several reasons, because I had misunderstood the situation and I got the impression that he was taken over the river Sava. But he was taken over the river Bosna, into Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Eventually he -- yes. It's right in the direction of. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, you said that Miroslav Tadic had the list of persons to be exchanged in his hands. Did Miroslav Tadic ever ask you whether you wanted to be exchanged, or did he ever issue instructions that everybody on the list had to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He didn't ask me whether I wished, and he said also that everybody has to be exchanged. He even shouted later that nobody should -- namely, if somebody decided not to, that the exchange would immediately be stopped. And I was -- we were the last, the last of the -- I was exchanged as a prisoner of war, and I learned that from the ICRC later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So you learnt about your status, your alleged status as a prisoner of war, from the ICRC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do I understand that at one stage someone from the ICRC asked you whether you wanted to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked me while I was in the secondary school in Bosanski Samac, and told me that I was a prisoner of war and whether I wished to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And the words that you said you heard Mr. Tadic utter about that everyone had to be exchanged or that the exchange would be immediately stopped, where did you hear him utter those words?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I heard it when I was on the truck, while we were on the truck, while the civilians were formed in lines according to the list, and at a certain point the exchange was stopped because somebody didn't want to go in. But then the exchange continued. I really don't know how that ended.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you know the person who had expressed a desire not to be included in the exchange?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I crossed, an elderly person didn't want to -- he wanted to return back. He was old, older. He wanted back, to go back. He said his wife remains, and he didn't know what was happening to his family, his wife, and the telephones weren't working. And he returned back to the boat, to be taken back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was he permitted to go back?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't allowed to return. They told him to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Who told him to go back, and where did they tell him to go back to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Here, on the bank. Those who were helping the elderly people, I don't know who the people were, but they brought him back to this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The people who brought the people back, were they from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: -- the Croatian side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, my learned friend. For the sake of clarity, it's a little bit confusing, all these questions and the answers. Maybe the witness could be directed to say which bank of the river, which side of these two sides. I mean, otherwise, we are a little bit in mist or fog. So maybe we can clarify that and then not to examine that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy. Can we have clarification from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. And with respect to my learned friend, I'm aware, reading the transcript, of where the inconsistencies are. The question I was midway through before he interrupted was exactly to clarify which people who brought him back were, and further, where they brought them back to. So I can do my job.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, the people who were helping the elderly people and brought this man back to the group, were they persons from the Croatian side or from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. So he tried to return from the Croatian side back to the Bosnian side -- back to the Serbian -- or the Serbian-controlled Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: But he was advised that they wouldn't allow him to return?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and they returned him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again, it's a problem, Your Honour. Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why don't you let her finish that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because in question, Your Honour, it's not clear and then obviously it's a misleading of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Pantelic. Will you sit down? Let Ms. Reidy proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I was just going to ask you a quick question. Whose decision was it in the end that, as best you know, that this gentleman should not stay in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, he already crossed from the Serbian side, at Zasavica, the Croatian village. Now, he crossed over to the Croatian side, and he wanted to return back on the Serbian side, from which he was originally transferred. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And why was he not allowed to return back to the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What, to the best of your information, prevented him from going back to the other side? Did you know if he was given any reason as to why he couldn't go back to the other side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He -- the exchange was already completed, and I was the last one to cross, and I met him when he was trying to go back, but it wasn't possible to go back any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Why was it not possible for him to go back any more?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Because he already crossed over, and they said themselves that there is no going back from where they had been -- we had been evicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It was the Croatian authorities who had told him that he wouldn't be -- they wouldn't -- he wouldn't be allowed back; is that it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did they say that they wouldn't allow him back or that he wouldn't be accepted back? And by "they," I mean the Croatian authorities. Did the Croatian authorities explain to him that they didn't want him to go back or that he would not be accepted back by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: They explained to him that he couldn't cross back on the other side because they wouldn't receive him there, and that everybody has crossed over to this side. And they had a hard time in convincing him to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time that this man had crossed over and you had crossed over, had Miroslav Tadic already told the group that everybody had to go, or that if one person didn't go, the exchange would be cancelled?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that while I was on that side, and he said it on that side.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: On "that side," do you mean the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break and resume our proceedings at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I'd like now to ask you some questions about the fate of the rest of your family, particularly I'd like to ask about how your wife and children were finally exchanged. Did your wife have to approach Miroslav Tadic in order to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife went to see him at least 20 times and begged him to be exchanged, Miroslav Tadic. Her name was erased off the list every time, and she was told she would not be exchanged. This is how it went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I need to ask you a question about this again, because there is a discrepancy between the English version and the version you signed, because an amendment you made was not incorporated into the English version. Can I ask you to look at paragraph 123 of your statement? You testified that your wife had been begged to be put on the list after you had been exchanged, and her name was erased off the list. Who actually physically told her or showed her the list with the name on it? Was it the defendant Miroslav Tadic, or was it another gentleman by the name of Velimir Maslic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The last time it was Miroslav -- it was Velimir Maslic. That was the last time. But prior to that she went to see Miroslav Tadic at least 20 times about the exchange, whereas Velimir Maslic told my wife she would never be exchanged as long as her husband continued shooting at their own children.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I draw your attention to this in paragraph 123. The second sentence, the second phrase of the second sentence reads: "Miroslav Tadic would refuse her permission to leave saying that I was shooting at them, that my family would not be allowed to go. They would let me shoot at my own children." And the witness had said that the person saying about the shooting was Velimir Maslic, and that was incorporated in the statement he signed. And unfortunately, it seems to have been overlooked in the English version. It wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The amendment was not incorporated. But I think the witness has made his position clear on who told his wife --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That she would never be exchanged. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Yes. In the same paragraph, 123, there is something odd about the second sentence: "I tried to get my wife on the list for a long time," although he was -- the witness was exchanged in May, and in paragraph 121, the last sentence reads: "I then fought with the HVO for 18 months." How did he try to get his wife on the list for a long time? I can't catch the meaning of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I'll ask the witness to explain to the Bench what you mean by trying to get your wife on the list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I remained with the HVO in order to be able to influence how the exchange lists were drawn up, because my wife, my children, my mother, my brother, who was in the camp, and my sister, remained in Samac. This is why I went to see various commissions and requested that my wife be put on the exchange list.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Is that clear, Your Honour? Would you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think a further clarification, yes. So does it mean that the various commissions he went to see were the commissions on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the Croatian side, they were both local and international ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And despite these efforts, you did -- you made to try to have your wife released from Bosanski Samac, did -- who would leave and did that decision depend, then, from her point of view, on Miroslav Tadic agreeing to her name on the list? Was that what she told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calling for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy has asked whether that's what his wife told her -- told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She actually said: What was the opinion of your wife? This was included in the question: What did your wife think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I must have missed it, because I thought --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: What I meant from her point of view, from her perspective, from her attempts, what did she tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, according to -- what she told the witness, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Although you were asking that she rejoin you, what did your wife tell you about who could give her permission to leave or not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: After seven months, my wife left Samac, and she told me that she went to see Miroslav Tadic at least 20 times, who did not want to give her permission to be exchanged, and that she was taken off the list on each occasion. She was told: You will not be exchanged. You are not on the list. Although I did put my wife's list -- my wife's name on the list. This is what my wife told me after she had been exchanged and after we reunited after seven months.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: So although you asked for your wife to join you and your wife wanted to join you, she was not free of her own will to do that when she wanted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And if and when she would be allowed to join you, that was controlled, as far as she experienced, by Miroslav Tadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: He was absolutely the one who decided who was to be allowed to go and who was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, I know that you did finally -- you were finally reunited with your family in November 1992. I want to ask you one final area, which is about the fate of some of your other relatives and what happened to them in Bosanski Samac, and in particular, I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 127 of your statement. In that, you stated that your mother-in-law was moved to Zasavica when, I presume, her son had swum across the River Sava in August 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but we're talking about her husband -- about her son. I'm sorry. About her son. He swam across the Sava River, and due to that, she was transferred to the camp in Zasavica, although she was over 70 or 75. She was even given a receipt for the items confiscated from her, the ones that she had on her at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask that the witness be shown a document? It's a document which the witness handed to the Prosecution. It's the one that he has just talked about and said that he has shown to us. It has been disclosed to the Defence. I also have the original with me, and I gave it to the Defence yesterday for inspection, and it's available for inspection by the members of the Bench as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is it called? What is the title of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The title of the document is "Receipt on temporary confiscation of objects," dated the 31st of August, 1992. An official translation is provided with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, can you see the document on the screen before you? It's also to the right of you, if you'd like to have a look. Is that document -- do you have a photocopy of the original document which your mother-in-law was given when she was removed from her home and sent to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document that I provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said I have the original document with me. I would like to be in a position for the witness and his family to keep it, but it is available for inspection by the Bench if they wish to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to be able to inspect the original receipt, because the last two lines that were typed on the typewriter - and this is a form - are not readable, not even in translation, and perhaps we would be able to establish what is written in the last two typewritten lines if we had the original. I see that even the translation doesn't reflect that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now talking about the form part, the part of this blank form that was typewritten. It's not legible. Perhaps the original is more legible than the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. I thought that the Prosecution had indicated -- had said that they had given the Defence the original for inspection.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it can just be handed to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Your Honour, while we are inspecting this document, there is certain discrepancy between B/C/S version and the English translation of this document. Namely, we don't know what is the content of the seal. If you see English version, there is only word "stamped." Maybe this witness can read slowly and then interpreters' unit can give us the idea what is the seal, in fact, here on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Ms. Reidy will go over that.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I'll cover that in the course of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, this person named in this -- as the recipient of this document is a Ms. Almasa Prljaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the name to whom the receipt was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And is that person your mother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my mother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think the contents of the document speak for itself. She was born on the 19th of October, 1919 which indeed make her over 70, on the date that this document was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether your mother-in-law ever received back any of these documents which this receipt indicates were taken from her?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: She never received any kind of receipt, neither did anybody else for the items that were confiscated from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what you have in front of you is a receipt for what was confiscated. What I wanted to know was whether or not she was ever returned the items listed from numbers 1 to 10 on this document.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No, they were never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have information as to whether all these documents were taken from your mother-in-law at her house when she was arrested or on her arrival in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: That was on the eve of her transfer to Zasavica, or just before her transfer to Zasavica, before they boarded the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to have a look at the seal, or the stamp, at the bottom of that document. And I have the original back, if you'd like to have a look at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps to waste time less, give the witness the original, assuming it's clearer than the photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: As best you're able, Mr. Jasarevic, could you read out what's written on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't have my glasses on, so I can't tell what is exactly written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honours, then, we would just get a separate translation of that stamp. I think it's a stamp we've seen on other documents and we can ask the Translation Unit to include it in their translation next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it now. "SAO Semberija and Majevica, Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac." So "SAO Semberija and Majevica." And right here it says: "Serbian Republic -- Serbian Republic and Serbian municipality Bosanski Samac, and SAO Semberija and Majevica," something "in the value of." I can't read the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Obviously, Your Honour, because this witness didn't read all the content of this seal, maybe the interpretation unit -- Translation Unit can provide us with the exact words which are in this seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Reidy.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll ask the Translation Unit to include it in the translation, stamp, and the full words will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, what was the fate of your mother-in-law after she was -- had been brought to Zasavica? Did she have to remain there or was she exchanged?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: She remained there until the very last exchange, I think. She remained in Zasavica. She was not allowed to go back to her own apartment, which had immediately been occupied by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to who the subsequent occupant was, or the ethnicity of that occupant?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The plate on my mother-in-law's apartment said "Djokic Bosar" [phoen], the wife of a fallen soldier. This is what it said on the door, and somebody else moved into her apartment and her things were not there any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall when this -- what you think might have been the last exchange was? Do you remember the date or the year?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I think it was in November. It was cold. 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: 1993. Thank you. I understand that some of your sisters had also been similarly evacuated or had been evicted from their flats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My sister was also evicted from her apartment. She couldn't even take her personal documents or any belongings. She had to leave the apartment in the clothes she had on at the time. She went to live, together with her son, in my mother's house. They even didn't let her son take some books with him. At the time he attended college.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Was your sister given any reason as to why she was evicted?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Somebody else moved in right away. They didn't even let her come close to the apartment any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: The person who moved into the flat, again, do you know who that person is or do you have any information as to the ethnicity of the person?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: By ethnicity, that person was a Serb. I don't know the name. He and his father came, and the father said, "Son, you deserve this. You deserved for somebody else to be evicted out of the apartment without the ability to take any of their belongings with them."

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: This exchange where you said the father came and said that the son deserved it, who had overheard this exchange?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: My sister was there present when the father said this. She was immediately thrown out and not allowed to make any comments. She wasn't allowed even to take with her basic necessities. They took everything away from her.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly when this occurred, when your sister was evicted from her flat?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but in the very beginning, among the first flats that were taken away in this manner. They would simply come and kick you out, and you had no right to do anything, just get out of there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could you give us a rough idea? Was it in 1992 or 1993, for example?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And was it prior to August 1992, if you can recall? And if you're not sure, just say it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Before August, yes. Before August.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And Mr. Jasarevic, the rest of your details about what happened to you and everything is in your statement. So I just want to ask -- and your statement also states that you were able to get your house back in recent years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I got my house back. My house was taken away just before my wife went to be exchanged. The day prior to that they came and took away the apartment and she had no right to go back to the apartment because she was to be exchanged the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did you -- have you moved back into your house and are you trying to rebuild your house in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I returned back to my apartment and renovated it, and now I'm living in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Did your family express their fear about your testimony here, given that you are now trying to -- or you've now renovated your house back in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My family is afraid, due to everything that we experienced in Bosanski Samac. When I returned to Bosanski Samac, I wasn't there for five days altogether when my dog was killed in my yard. I reported this to the police. The police didn't do anything. They simply interrogated me and they never found the person who killed the dog. My neighbour was there, and everybody knows who did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I've finished my examination-in-chief, and the witness is available for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have this receipt numbered for identification, pending the translation of the stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It will be P130 ID and P130 ter ID. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, could I just raise very briefly one matter that arose this morning? I'm certainly not opening the topic again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But in the course of submissions, Mr. Lukic stood up and said: "The Defence is prepared to allow its witnesses who will come here to testify under Rule 92 bis to be cross-examined immediately and not to be examined in chief first." So he has made his position clear. That's the way the Defence case is going to be conducted. I wonder if, because having read the passage, he seemed to be speaking for all Defence counsel. I wonder if now Mr. Pisarevic or Mr. Pantelic could indicate if they also will be presenting their Defence case in that fashion that Mr. Lukic so clearly and comprehensively set out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was quite clear. I said that in the sense that both sides have equality of arms, an equal equality of arms. However, if the Prosecution has the right of direct examination, I, for my witnesses, will avail myself of the right for our witnesses. I only make this proposal in order to speed up the process, to save on time. And I didn't do this on behalf of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I don't want to take up time now, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are going to have a pre-Defence Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay. Well, may I simply say that I strongly suggest Mr. Lukic reread, and other Defence counsel reread page 50, line 20 through to page 51, line 12, because I certainly don't intend to let them forget that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. Obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I've said that we are going to deal with that at the pre-Defence conference, and I don't want to waste time any more. We have a witness on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jasarevic. My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm a lawyer, and I am present here on behalf of the defence of Mr. Tadic, and I will be carrying out the cross here. I shall try to formulate the questions so that you'll be able to answer them with a "yes," or a "no," or "I don't know," and if need be -- an additional explanation will be needed, I will directly ask you for such a further explanation. Mr. Jasarevic, in your statement, as well as in your testimony today, at the question of the Prosecution, you mentioned that you saw, in front of and around the Cafe AS, members of the 4th Detachment and of the special units. You also stated that you were passing by the Cafe AS when going to work and when returning from work. And when questioned by the Prosecutor the time frame and when you observed these people, the Prosecutor said that it was at the end of 1991 and at the beginning of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I knew all the members of the 4th Detachment, and I saw the special units only on the eve of the attack on Bosanski Samac, in front of the AS Cafe, when I was returning from work. I made that statement. I said that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say the 16th or the 17th?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: The 17th -- 16th. No, the 17th was the attack. 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see the members of the special units before that in front and around Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them earlier, because I didn't know them. There were people I did not know. But I did see them before, at the rallies throughout the town, the peace rally in the cinema, and I did recognise them when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Whom did you see of the special units at the peace rally?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: I saw him, Slobodan Miljkovic, Lugar. He was in a white tracksuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that as a white tracksuit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When was that? Can you remember, approximately prior to 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: It must have been six, seven days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The person in a white tracksuit, wasn't he maybe Boric Stanko, known as Borac?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No. He was Lugar, and I recognised him when Dikan was killed, and we all discussed Slobodan Miljkovic, Lugar, in a white Adidas tracksuit. That is how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasarevic, in your statement, paragraph 14, you mentioned the 4th Detachment. You said it was formed by the JNA and that a Yugoslav flag was flying in front of Mladost?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that the headquarters of the 4th Detachment was there, its office.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a temporary headquarters. Later it moved, because they couldn't usurp the facilities of others, and it was moved to the AS Cafe owned by Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Compared to Mladost, where is Cafe AS?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: Cafe AS is right across the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Was it usual in 1992, in Samac, that people who work in a company or that they have an association and that they meet in the neighbouring cafe? Would that be unusual?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN JASAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the 4th Detachment was in Mladost. When was the command moved from Mladost to AS?
